NOTES AND QUESTIONS
1. The interplay between preliminary injunctions and TROs was on display in one of the earliest cases involving the Trump Administration’s ban
on travel by noncitizens from designated countries. Following the signing of Executive Order 13769, the states of Washington and Minnesota sought a
TRO enjoining enforcement of the ban. After a district court granted the TRO, the government quickly appealed to the Ninth Circuit. Plaintiff-
appellees challenged the appellate court’s jurisdiction and ability to review the TRO. However, the court found that because of the government’s
vigorous defense of the ban, the TRO was effectively a preliminary injunction, and was reviewable. See Washington v. Trump, 847 F.3d 1151, 1158
(9th Cir. 2017), cert. denied, 138 S.Ct. 448, 199 L.Ed.2d 331 (2017).
2.In some cases plaintiff may seek a preliminary injunction that mandates the taking of action, rather than prohibiting it. A classic discussion of
mandatory injunctions appears in then-Judge William Howard Taft’s opinion in TOLEDO, A.A. & N.M. RY. v. PENNSYLVANIA CO., 54 Fed. 730,
741 (C.C.N.D. Ohio), appeal dismissed, 150 U.S. 393, 14 S.Ct. 123, 37 L.Ed. 1120 (1893):
The office of a preliminary injunction is to preserve the status quo until, upon final hearing, the court may grant full relief. Generally this
can be accomplished by an injunction prohibitory in form, but it sometimes happens that the status quo is a condition not of rest, but of
action, and the condition of rest is exactly what will inflict the irreparable injury upon complainant, which he appeals to a court of equity to
protect him from. In such a case courts of equity issue mandatory writs before the case is heard on its merits. * * *
When a mandatory preliminary injunction may go beyond maintaining the status quo, the standard for its issuance is higher. See Tom Doherty
Associates, Inc. v. Saban Entertainment, Inc., 60 F.3d 27 (2d Cir. 1995). As the Ninth Circuit has explained, “[w]here a party seeks mandatory
preliminary relief that goes well beyond maintaining the status quo pendente lite, courts should be extremely cautious about issuing a preliminary
injunction.” Martin v. International Olympic Committee, 740 F.2d 670, 675 (9th Cir. 1984). Thus,
